screens.title: IPv6 Addressing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn why IPv6 replaced IPv4, how its 128-bit addresses are written and shortened, and how devices obtain addresses automatically. IPv6 solves the address exhaustion problem by using a much larger address space — 128 bits — which removes the need for many address-sharing workarounds. You'll also learn the notation rules: hexadecimal groups separated by colons, omitting leading zeros, and compressing consecutive zero segments with a double colon only once. We'll map those rules to concrete examples so you can shorten and expand real addresses without error. Next, we'll examine address types you will see as a support technician: Global Unicast, Link-Local, Unique Local, Multicast, and Anycast. Finally, you'll follow the stateless autoconfiguration flow—how a host uses EUI-64 to build an interface identifier from a MAC address, and how a router advertisement supplies the network prefix so the host can form a full global address. This chapter mixes concept cards, terminal-style command examples, and hands-on exercises so you can both recognize addresses and simulate configuration safely. By the end you will be able to read IPv6 output, shorten addresses correctly, and explain SLAAC versus DHCPv6.

screens.title: Why IPv6? Address exhaustion and advantages
screens.narratorSegment: IPv6 exists because the original IPv4 addressing model could not scale to the number of devices on modern networks. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, giving about 4.3 billion unique addresses — a limit we've effectively reached for public routable addresses. IPv6 expands that field to 128 bits, producing roughly 3.4 times 10 to the 38 addresses. That increase changes how networks are designed: you no longer need large-scale NAT to share addresses, and you can assign globally routable addresses more widely. Beyond raw space, IPv6 designs in other improvements: a streamlined header for more efficient routing and built-in support for IPsec, which was optional in IPv4. For a support technician, the practical outcomes are important. You will see fewer address-sharing workarounds, and many devices will obtain addresses automatically via SLAAC, so your troubleshooting shifts from NAT mapping to verifying prefixes and router advertisements. A common misconception is that IPv6 is simply 'longer IPv4'—but it's also an operational shift: autoconfiguration, link-local dependencies, and new address scopes matter for reachability and diagnostics. To check if IPv6 is in use on a host, use the read-only commands shown in the lab; recognizing when an address is GUA versus LLA helps you target the right troubleshooting step. Consider this: if you can see a FE80 address and no GUA, your issue may be routing or missing router advertisements rather than an addressing shortage.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Why IPv6?
From 32 bits to 128 bits
IPv6 increases available addresses dramatically and changes network operations.
Key advantage: address space
IPv4: ~4.3 billion addresses. IPv6: about 3.4 x 10^38 addresses — enough to avoid large-scale NAT for most designs.
Operational changes
Autoconfiguration becomes common (SLAAC), and link-local addressing is always present for local operations.
Common misconception
IPv6 isn't only longer addresses — it introduces new behavior like mandatory link-local addresses and different troubleshooting steps.
Key Takeaway

IPv6 gives huge address space and changes address management. Learn to spot scope and autoconfiguration as your primary troubleshooting signals.

Illustrative example
2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334
This single address format already shows why hex and grouping matter. Shortening makes it readable.
Support technician angle
  • Look for FE80 addresses to diagnose local link issues.
  • If only LLA exists, check for router advertisements before suspecting routing.
  • Recognize GUA prefixes to determine global reachability.

screens.title: IPv6 address format and hexadecimal notation
screens.narratorSegment: An IPv6 address is a 128-bit number typically written as eight 16-bit groups in hexadecimal, separated by colons. Each hexadecimal digit represents four bits, so a group of four hex digits is a 16-bit segment. For example, the canonical form 2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334 contains eight groups of four hex digits. Hexadecimal is used because it compactly represents binary data: every hex digit maps to four bits, so it reduces the visual length compared to binary while remaining precise. As a support technician, you must be comfortable reading these groups and understanding which part of an address is the network prefix versus the interface identifier. Typically network prefixes are expressed with a slash notation like /64, indicating the leftmost 64 bits are the network portion. A concrete example: when you see 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64 in a router advertisement, the /64 tells you the host will use the remaining 64 bits as its interface identifier. A misconception is treating each colon-separated element as independent addresses; they are segments of a single 128-bit value. Practice converting small hex groups mentally and identify the prefix length from configuration output — this will speed up diagnosing prefix mismatches or misapplied addresses.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Address Format
Hexadecimal groups and prefix length
Each hex digit is 4 bits; four hex digits make a 16-bit segment. Prefix length indicates how many leftmost bits are network bits.
Canonical example
2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334
Practical note
Routers use prefix notation like /64 to tell hosts which bits form the network. SLAAC commonly relies on a /64 network prefix to combine with a 64-bit interface identifier.
Small conversion example
Hex to bits: DB8 = D(13) B(11) 8(8) → 1101 1011 1000 — each hex digit maps to 4 bits, which helps you verify prefix boundaries.
Support tip
  • Recognize common prefix markers like 2000::/3 for Global Unicast networks.
  • Expect /64 networks for SLAAC; if prefix length differs, autoconfiguration behavior changes.

screens.title: Shortening IPv6 addresses
screens.narratorSegment: Shortening IPv6 addresses reduces visual clutter but must follow precise rules. Rule one: omit leading zeros within each 16-bit segment. For example, 0DB8 becomes DB8 and 0000 becomes 0. Rule two: compress a single longest contiguous run of one or more 16-bit zero segments using a double colon '::'. You may only use '::' once per address to avoid ambiguity. When multiple equal-length runs exist, pick one to compress — consistency and clarity guide your choice. A concrete example from the chapter: 2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334 becomes 2001:DB8:85A3::8A2E:370:7334 after omitting leading zeros and compressing the two zero segments in the middle. A common error is inserting '::' twice, which creates an ambiguous address. Another pitfall is compressing a single zero segment unnecessarily when there are longer runs available — always compress the longest contiguous run to produce the shortest unambiguous representation. For troubleshooting, when you see a shortened form in device output, expand it mentally or on paper to confirm the prefix and interface identifier match expected values. Practicing with the provided examples will build accuracy quickly. Shortening IPv6 addresses means omit leading zeros and compress the longest contiguous zero run once with '::'. never use '::' more than once.. In practical terms, rules for omitting leading zeros and compressing zeros using ::. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Shortening Rules
Two rules to shorten safely
Omit leading zeros inside segments. Compress the longest sequence of all-zero segments once with '::'.
Rule 1: Omit leading zeros
0DB8 → DB8; 0000 → 0
Rule 2: Compress longest zero run
Replace a contiguous set of all-zero 16-bit segments with '::' once per address.
Pitfall
Using '::' more than once is invalid and creates ambiguity.
Worked example
Original: 2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334 Step 1: Omit leading zeros → 2001:DB8:85A3:0:0:8A2E:370:7334 Step 2: Compress largest zero run → 2001:DB8:85A3::8A2E:370:7334
Check your understanding
If you see 2001:DB8::1, expand it to find which segments are omitted and confirm the prefix length if given.

screens.title: IPv6 Address Types
screens.narratorSegment: IPv6 divides addresses by how packets are delivered. Unicast addresses identify a single interface; packets sent to a unicast address are delivered only to that interface. Within unicast, Global Unicast Addresses are globally routable and typically start with 2000::/3, Link-Local Addresses start with FE80::/10 and are valid only on the local link, and Unique Local Addresses start with FC00::/7 and are for site-local private use. Multicast addresses identify a group of interfaces; a packet sent to a multicast address is delivered to all members of that group and multicast addresses begin with FF00::/8. Anycast addresses also identify a group, but routers deliver a packet to the nearest interface in that group according to routing metrics. A concrete example: a router advertisement might use a GUA prefix for global traffic while neighbor discovery uses LLAs for link-only operations. A common misconception is confusing Link-Local addresses with ULAs; LLAs cannot be routed beyond the local segment and are essential for functions like neighbor discovery and router solicitation. Recognizing these types in logs or command output — by their common prefixes — helps you determine whether an address should be reachable beyond the immediate network or not. When diagnosing reachability, always first verify if the destination address is link-local, unique local, or global to narrow your investigation.

keyIdea.text: Address type determines reachability: LLAs for local link operations, GUAs for global reachability, ULAs for internal use, multicast for groups, and anycast for nearest delivery.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Address Types
Unicast, Multicast, Anycast
Delivery semantics determine the address type and expected behavior when you troubleshoot reachability.
Unicast
Delivers to a single interface. GUAs start with 2000::/3, LLAs with FE80::/10, ULAs with FC00::/7.
Multicast
Delivers to all members of a group. Multicast prefixes start with FF00::/8.
Anycast
Assigned to multiple interfaces; routing delivers to the nearest one. Common for distributed services.
Quick reference
GUA: 2000::/3 • LLA: FE80::/10 • ULA: FC00::/7 • Multicast: FF00::/8
Scenario
If a host can ping a neighbor's FE80 address but not a GUA, the problem likely involves routing or router advertisements rather than the host's address configuration.

screens.title: Global Unicast, Link-Local, and Unique Local Addresses
screens.narratorSegment: Unicast addresses are the ones you'll most commonly check as a support technician, and understanding the subtypes helps you decide whether communication should be local or global. Global Unicast Addresses are globally routable and typically fall under 2000::/3. If a device has a GUA, it can potentially reach the public internet if routing and firewall policies allow it. Link-Local Addresses always start with FE80::/10 and are automatically configured on every IPv6-enabled interface. LLAs are only valid on the local network segment and are used for neighbor discovery, router solicitation, and other essential link-local functions. Unique Local Addresses start with FC00::/7 and behave like private IPv4 addresses: they're for internal organization use and not intended to be routed on the public internet. A concrete example: a device might have an LLA for neighbor operations, a GUA for internet access, and a ULA for internal resources; these can coexist on the same interface. A common misconception is assuming LLAs are optional — in practice, they are foundational to local IPv6 operations. When troubleshooting, identify the prefix and then apply the correct validation steps: check RAs for GUAs, check local neighbor tables for LLAs, and treat ULAs like private addresses when diagnosing reachability beyond your administrative domain.

keyIdea.title: Unicast subtypes
keyIdea.text: GUA = global reachability, LLA = link-only, ULA = private internal. Devices often have multiple addresses for different scopes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Unicast Subtypes
GUA, LLA, ULA explained
Recognize prefixes and intended scopes to narrow troubleshooting quickly.
Global Unicast (GUA)
Typically start with 2000::/3. Routable on the internet when permitted by routing and policy.
Link-Local (LLA)
Start with FE80::/10. Auto-configured and essential for local link functions like ND and RS/RA.
Unique Local (ULA)
Start with FC00::/7. Private to an organization, not for global routing.
Real-world check
# Example display on a host fe80::21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e/64 (Link-Local) 2001:db8:abcd:1::1234/64 (Global Unicast) fc00:db8::10/64 (Unique Local)
Troubleshooting tip
If a server has only a ULA and clients on the internet cannot reach it, that behavior is expected because ULAs are not globally routable.

screens.title: SLAAC: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
screens.narratorSegment: SLAAC lets a host create its own IPv6 address without a DHCP server. The process begins with the host generating a Link-Local Address, often using the EUI-64 method to derive a 64-bit interface identifier from the MAC address. Once the LLA exists, the host sends a Router Solicitation to discover routers on the link. A router replies with a Router Advertisement containing one or more network prefixes, for example 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64. The host then combines that advertised network prefix with its interface identifier to form a Global Unicast Address. This is stateless because routers do not keep a mapping of which host received which address; each host generates its own identifier deterministically. A common misconception is that SLAAC provides every configuration detail — it does not. SLAAC supplies the address and basic parameters, but not always DNS servers; DHCPv6 may be used in conjunction for those settings. Another frequent troubleshooting observation is a host with an LLA but no GUA; this often indicates the absence of router advertisements or misconfigured prefixes. When diagnosing SLAAC issues, confirm the presence of RAs and ensure prefix lengths like /64 are appropriate for hosts to construct valid global addresses.

narration.text: SLAAC lets a host create its own IPv6 address without a DHCP server. The process begins with the host generating a Link-Local Address, often using the EUI-64 method to derive a 64-bit interface identifier from the MAC address. Once the LLA exists, the host sends a Router Solicitation to discover routers on the link. A router replies with a Router Advertisement containing one or more network prefixes, for example 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64. The host then combines that advertised network prefix with its interface identifier to form a Global Unicast Address. This is stateless because routers do not keep a mapping of which host received which address; each host generates its own identifier deterministically. A common misconception is that SLAAC provides every configuration detail — it does not. SLAAC supplies the address and basic parameters, but not always DNS servers; DHCPv6 may be used in conjunction for those settings. Another frequent troubleshooting observation is a host with an LLA but no GUA; this often indicates the absence of router advertisements or misconfigured prefixes. When diagnosing SLAAC issues, confirm the presence of RAs and ensure prefix lengths like /64 are appropriate for hosts to construct valid global addresses.

keyIdea.title: SLAAC summary
keyIdea.text: Host forms an LLA, requests RAs, receives a prefix, and combines it with its interface ID to build a global address — stateless and host-driven.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › SLAAC Flow
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
SLAAC allows hosts to form addresses autonomously after receiving router advertisements.
Step 1: LLA generation
Host generates a link-local address (FE80::/10), often using EUI-64.
Step 2: Router Solicitation / Advertisement
Host sends RS; routers reply with RA containing prefix and flags.
Step 3: Form global address
Host combines RA prefix (e.g., /64) with its 64-bit IID to create the GUA.
Example RA prefix
2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64
A host receiving this RA will use the left 64 bits as the network portion and generate or reuse its 64-bit IID.
Misconception check
SLAAC does not always supply DNS addresses. Use DHCPv6 in stateful or stateless mode if DNS must be assigned centrally.

screens.title: EUI-64: Building a 64-bit interface identifier
screens.narratorSegment: EUI-64 is a deterministic method to derive a 64-bit interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC address so hosts can generate consistent IPv6 addresses. The basic steps are: split the 48-bit MAC address into two 24-bit halves, insert the fixed 16-bit sequence FFFE in the middle, and flip the seventh bit of the first byte (the Universal/Local bit). For example, given MAC 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E, you split into 001A2B and 3C4D5E, insert FFFE between them to become 001A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E, then flip the 7th bit of the first octet which changes the binary in that position to indicate local scope as needed. The result is a 64-bit interface identifier that is highly likely to be unique on the local link. One misconception is that EUI-64 always uses the MAC exactly as-is; in reality the U/L bit flip is required and insertion of FFFE is mandatory for the standard method. As a support technician, knowing EUI-64 helps you map observed interface identifiers back to device MACs when analyzing host addresses and duplicates on a link. If privacy extensions are enabled, the host may use randomized IIDs instead of EUI-64 to improve tracking resistance.

keyIdea.title: EUI-64 process
keyIdea.text: Split MAC, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit — this creates a 64-bit IID used with a /64 prefix for SLAAC addresses.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › EUI-64
EUI-64 explained
A standard way to convert a 48-bit MAC into a 64-bit interface identifier for SLAAC.
Step A: Split MAC
Divide the 48-bit MAC into two 24-bit halves.
Step B: Insert FFFE
Insert the fixed 16-bit value FFFE in the middle of the halves.
Step C: Flip the U/L bit
Toggle the 7th bit of the first octet to finalize the IID.
Worked example
MAC: 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E Split: 001A2B / 3C4D5E Insert FFFE: 001A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E Flip 7th bit: final IID: 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
Interpretation
This IID appended to FE80::/64 produces the device LLA and can combine with an RA prefix to form a global address.

screens.title: Router Advertisement and forming the Global Address
screens.narratorSegment: Router Advertisements are the messages routers send on a link to tell hosts about available prefixes and configuration flags. When a router advertises a prefix such as 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64, hosts can use SLAAC to combine that prefix with their 64-bit interface identifier — whether derived via EUI-64 or chosen by privacy extensions — to form a Global Unicast Address. The RA also includes flags that indicate whether hosts should use DHCPv6 for additional configuration or rely on SLAAC alone. A practical example: a host generates an IID and receives RA with a /64 prefix; it concatenates the prefix and IID to produce a full 128-bit address. Misunderstandings arise when the advertised prefix length is not a /64; many SLAAC implementations assume a /64 and may not form addresses if the prefix differs. As a technician, inspect RA content and prefix lengths when hosts have no GUAs or mismatched addresses. Also remember that RA-driven addresses are stateless: routers don't track who took which address. If you need centralized assignment of DNS servers or other options, DHCPv6 in stateful or stateless mode is the complement to RAs and SLAAC.

keyIdea.title: RA role
keyIdea.text: Router Advertisements provide prefixes and flags; hosts combine an RA prefix with an IID to generate a global address under SLAAC.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Router Advertisement
How RAs form the global address
Router Advertisements supply prefixes and flags that hosts use with their IID to create GUAs.
RA contains:
Network prefix, prefix length, and flags indicating SLAAC/DHCPv6 usage.
Host action
Combine RA prefix (left 64 bits) with IID (right 64 bits) to form a full address under SLAAC.
Example RA prefix
2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64
The host will append its IID to this 64-bit prefix to create the GUA.
Troubleshooting hint
If a host has an LLA but no GUA, verify RAs are present and advertising a usable /64 prefix; also check RA flags for DHCPv6 requirements.

screens.title: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
screens.narratorSegment: SLAAC and DHCPv6 are complementary mechanisms for IPv6 configuration. SLAAC is stateless and enables each host to construct its own address by combining an advertised prefix with an IID, while DHCPv6 provides centralized control and can operate in stateful or stateless modes. In stateful DHCPv6, the server assigns full addresses and maintains a record of leases — similar to traditional DHCP for IPv4. In stateless DHCPv6, DHCPv6 supplies auxiliary configuration like DNS servers while addresses remain SLAAC-derived. Use DHCPv6 when you require centralized assignment of DNS or strict administrative mapping of addresses. Use SLAAC when you prefer decentralized, low-overhead address configuration that scales without maintaining server-side state. A practical troubleshooting insight: if clients lack DNS information but have correct GUAs, check whether DHCPv6 is expected and whether RAs indicated that SLAAC-only should be used. Misunderstandings often arise when administrators assume SLAAC supplies DNS settings — it does not reliably do so, which is why DHCPv6 stateless mode is common for DNS provisioning. Choose the method that matches your policy and tooling, and confirm RA flags and DHCPv6 server reachability during diagnostics.

keyIdea.title: Which to use
keyIdea.text: SLAAC is decentralized address generation; DHCPv6 is used when centralized control or DNS assignment is required. They can operate together.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › SLAAC vs DHCPv6
Compare configuration models
SLAAC = stateless host-driven. DHCPv6 = central server-driven or stateless DNS provisioning.
SLAAC
Autoconfigures addresses using RA prefixes and IIDs. No server state required.
DHCPv6 (Stateful)
Server assigns addresses and keeps lease state. Useful for strict control.
DHCPv6 (Stateless)
Provides configuration like DNS while addresses are SLAAC-derived.
Diagnostic example
If hosts have GUAs but no DNS, DHCPv6 stateless mode or DNS settings are likely missing — check DHCPv6 reachability and RA flags.
Best practice
Use SLAAC for scale and simplicity; add DHCPv6 when you need centralized options like DNS assignment or inventorying addresses.

screens.title: Hands-on: Shortening examples and terminal checks
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walkthrough gives you two practical tasks you can perform safely in a virtual environment. Task one: shorten several example addresses step-by-step using the rules we've covered. Practice on: 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:FF00:0042:8329, FE80:0000:0000:0000:0202:B3FF:FE1E:8329, and 2001:0DB8:AC10:0001:0000:0000:0000:0050. For each, omit leading zeros and compress the longest zero runs to produce an unambiguous shortened form. Task two: view IPv6 addresses on your test machine without changing configuration. On Windows run the read-only command to list interface IPv6 addresses. On Linux run the ip -6 command. The commands below are safe read-only examples you can copy into a lab terminal. Observe how LLAs, GUAs, and ULAs appear and map to prefixes. A common mistake during the exercise is applying '::' twice; if you see unexpected results, expand the shortened address back to full form to check where zeros were compressed. These exercises help you move from recognition to fluent use so you can quickly interpret real device output during troubleshooting. Hands-on: Shortening examples and terminal checks means shorten the example addresses correctly and run read-only commands to view ipv6 assignments in a safe test environment.. In practical terms, practice shortening and run read-only commands to view ipv6 addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Hands-on Lab
Shortening exercises
Work through these addresses using omission and compression rules.
Addresses to shorten
2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:FF00:0042:8329
FE80:0000:0000:0000:0202:B3FF:FE1E:8329

screens.title: Simulated configuration commands
screens.narratorSegment: When you need to practice adding or removing addresses, always do so in a virtual machine or isolated lab. The chapter supplies example commands you can use to add a test Unique Local Address for practice and then remove it. On Windows the netsh interface ipv6 add address command lets you add a ULA like FC00:DB8::10/64 to an interface named 'Ethernet' and later delete it. On Linux you can use sudo ip -6 addr add and sudo ip -6 addr del to perform the same actions against eth0. These commands change system settings, so the guidance emphasizes testing in VMs only. A typical workflow: check current addresses with the read-only command, add the temporary ULA for testing, confirm it appears, then remove it to restore the original state. A common mistake is failing to remove test addresses and leaving stale configuration on a production NIC, so always delete test addresses after verification. Use ULAs for testing to avoid accidental global routing, and record what you changed so you can revert cleanly. Practicing these steps builds confidence reading output and understanding how address lifecycles behave on real systems.

keyIdea.text: Add/delete addresses only in test environments; use ULAs for practice and always remove test addresses afterward.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Simulated Configuration
Safe add/delete examples
Use these commands only in a lab or VM. Prefer ULA addresses for tests.
Windows (example)
# View current IPv6 addresses
netsh interface ipv6 show addresses "Ethernet"

# Add a test ULA (requires admin)
# netsh interface ipv6 add address "Ethernet" FC00:DB8::10/64

# Delete test ULA
# netsh interface ipv6 delete address "Ethernet" FC00:DB8::10
Linux (example)
# View current IPv6 addresses
ip -6 a show eth0

# Add a test ULA (requires root)
# sudo ip -6 addr add FC00:DB8::10/64 dev eth0

# Delete test ULA
# sudo ip -6 addr del FC00:DB8::10/64 dev eth0
Post-check
After adding, re-run the view command to confirm the address appears. After testing, delete it and verify it's removed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the essential concepts you need to keep practicing. First, IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written as eight hexadecimal groups; this enormous address space removes many of the scaling problems of IPv4. Second, shortening rules let you omit leading zeros and compress one longest contiguous run of zero segments with '::' only once — misuse leads to ambiguity. Third, recognize address types by prefix: GUA (2000::/3) for global routing, LLA (FE80::/10) for link-local operations, and ULA (FC00::/7) for private internal use. Fourth, SLAAC plus EUI-64 enable stateless autoconfiguration: a host builds a link-local from its MAC, solicits routers, receives a prefix, and combines that prefix with its IID to form a global address. Finally, DHCPv6 complements SLAAC when centralized configuration or DNS assignment is needed. As you practice with the provided shortening examples and safe terminal commands, focus on identifying scope and prefix lengths — those are the fastest clues to why an IPv6 address is or isn't reachable. Keep testing in a VM and always remove test addresses after you finish.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn why IPv6 replaced IPv4, how its 128-bit addresses are written and shortened, and how devices obtain addresses automatically. IPv6 solves the address exhaustion problem by using a much larger address space — 128 bits — which removes the need for many address-sharing workarounds. You'll also learn the notation rules: hexadecimal groups separated by colons, omitting leading zeros, and compressing consecutive zero segments with a double colon only once. We'll map those rules to concrete examples so you can shorten and expand real addresses without error. Next, we'll examine address types you will see as a support technician: Global Unicast, Link-Local, Unique Local, Multicast, and Anycast. Finally, you'll follow the stateless autoconfiguration flow—how a host uses EUI-64 to build an interface identifier from a MAC address, and how a router advertisement supplies the network prefix so the host can form a full global address. This chapter mixes concept cards, terminal-style command examples, and hands-on exercises so you can both recognize addresses and simulate configuration safely. By the end you will be able to read IPv6 output, shorten addresses correctly, and explain SLAAC versus DHCPv6.

These objectives guide the practice you'll do across the chapter. First, you'll explain why IPv6 is necessary and identify the advantages it brings, including a vastly larger address space and built-in support for security features. Second, you'll read, write, and correctly shorten IPv6 addresses using hexadecimal notation, omitting leading zeros, and compressing consecutive zero segments without creating ambiguity. Third, you'll identify Unicast, Multicast, and Anycast addresses and recognize common subtypes like Global Unicast, Link-Local, and Unique Local addresses by their prefixes. Fourth, you'll understand SLAAC and the EUI-64 process so you can explain how a host generates a link-local and then a global address when it receives a router advertisement. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding with practical checks and short terminal commands. These skills matter because as a support technician you'll read device output, decide whether an address is locally scoped or globally routable, and troubleshoot misconfigured shortening or autoconfiguration issues. By the end of the chapter, you should be able to explain each objective and demonstrate it in a simple simulated environment.

Beyond understanding, you will practice two concrete skills. First, shortening and expanding addresses: you will take full addresses and apply the leading-zero omission and zero compression rules so your shortened answer is correct and unambiguous. Second, simulated configuration: you'll run simple read-only commands in a terminal on Windows or Linux to observe IPv6 addresses and verify whether a host has a Link-Local or Global address. The practice includes exercises such as shortening specific example addresses and safely adding or removing a ULA on a test interface in a virtual environment. These verification steps matter because real troubleshooting begins with reading the output of 'ip -6 a' or 'netsh interface ipv6 show addresses' and recognizing whether an address is local-only or globally routable. Finally, the milestone for this screen is performing the two practice tasks without changing production interfaces: shorten three example addresses correctly and run the read-only command to show current IPv6 addresses in your test environment. This ensures you can both reason about addresses and use basic tools to confirm what you see on devices.

IPv6 exists because the original IPv4 addressing model could not scale to the number of devices on modern networks. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, giving about 4.3 billion unique addresses — a limit we've effectively reached for public routable addresses. IPv6 expands that field to 128 bits, producing roughly 3.4 times 10 to the 38 addresses. That increase changes how networks are designed: you no longer need large-scale NAT to share addresses, and you can assign globally routable addresses more widely. Beyond raw space, IPv6 designs in other improvements: a streamlined header for more efficient routing and built-in support for IPsec, which was optional in IPv4. For a support technician, the practical outcomes are important. You will see fewer address-sharing workarounds, and many devices will obtain addresses automatically via SLAAC, so your troubleshooting shifts from NAT mapping to verifying prefixes and router advertisements. A common misconception is that IPv6 is simply 'longer IPv4'—but it's also an operational shift: autoconfiguration, link-local dependencies, and new address scopes matter for reachability and diagnostics. To check if IPv6 is in use on a host, use the read-only commands shown in the lab; recognizing when an address is GUA versus LLA helps you target the right troubleshooting step. Consider this: if you can see a FE80 address and no GUA, your issue may be routing or missing router advertisements rather than an addressing shortage.

An IPv6 address is a 128-bit number typically written as eight 16-bit groups in hexadecimal, separated by colons. Each hexadecimal digit represents four bits, so a group of four hex digits is a 16-bit segment. For example, the canonical form 2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334 contains eight groups of four hex digits. Hexadecimal is used because it compactly represents binary data: every hex digit maps to four bits, so it reduces the visual length compared to binary while remaining precise. As a support technician, you must be comfortable reading these groups and understanding which part of an address is the network prefix versus the interface identifier. Typically network prefixes are expressed with a slash notation like /64, indicating the leftmost 64 bits are the network portion. A concrete example: when you see 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64 in a router advertisement, the /64 tells you the host will use the remaining 64 bits as its interface identifier. A misconception is treating each colon-separated element as independent addresses; they are segments of a single 128-bit value. Practice converting small hex groups mentally and identify the prefix length from configuration output — this will speed up diagnosing prefix mismatches or misapplied addresses.

Shortening IPv6 addresses reduces visual clutter but must follow precise rules. Rule one: omit leading zeros within each 16-bit segment. For example, 0DB8 becomes DB8 and 0000 becomes 0. Rule two: compress a single longest contiguous run of one or more 16-bit zero segments using a double colon '::'. You may only use '::' once per address to avoid ambiguity. When multiple equal-length runs exist, pick one to compress — consistency and clarity guide your choice. A concrete example from the chapter: 2001:0DB8:85A3:0000:0000:8A2E:0370:7334 becomes 2001:DB8:85A3::8A2E:370:7334 after omitting leading zeros and compressing the two zero segments in the middle. A common error is inserting '::' twice, which creates an ambiguous address. Another pitfall is compressing a single zero segment unnecessarily when there are longer runs available — always compress the longest contiguous run to produce the shortest unambiguous representation. For troubleshooting, when you see a shortened form in device output, expand it mentally or on paper to confirm the prefix and interface identifier match expected values. Practicing with the provided examples will build accuracy quickly. Shortening IPv6 addresses means omit leading zeros and compress the longest contiguous zero run once with '::'. never use '::' more than once.. In practical terms, rules for omitting leading zeros and compressing zeros using ::. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. IPv6 divides addresses by how packets are delivered. Unicast addresses identify a single interface; packets sent to a unicast address are delivered only to that interface. Within unicast, Global Unicast Addresses are globally routable and typically start with 2000::/3, Link-Local Addresses start with FE80::/10 and are valid only on the local link, and Unique Local Addresses start with FC00::/7 and are for site-local private use. Multicast addresses identify a group of interfaces; a packet sent to a multicast address is delivered to all members of that group and multicast addresses begin with FF00::/8. Anycast addresses also identify a group, but routers deliver a packet to the nearest interface in that group according to routing metrics. A concrete example: a router advertisement might use a GUA prefix for global traffic while neighbor discovery uses LLAs for link-only operations. A common misconception is confusing Link-Local addresses with ULAs; LLAs cannot be routed beyond the local segment and are essential for functions like neighbor discovery and router solicitation. Recognizing these types in logs or command output — by their common prefixes — helps you determine whether an address should be reachable beyond the immediate network or not. When diagnosing reachability, always first verify if the destination address is link-local, unique local, or global to narrow your investigation.

Unicast addresses are the ones you'll most commonly check as a support technician, and understanding the subtypes helps you decide whether communication should be local or global. Global Unicast Addresses are globally routable and typically fall under 2000::/3. If a device has a GUA, it can potentially reach the public internet if routing and firewall policies allow it. Link-Local Addresses always start with FE80::/10 and are automatically configured on every IPv6-enabled interface. LLAs are only valid on the local network segment and are used for neighbor discovery, router solicitation, and other essential link-local functions. Unique Local Addresses start with FC00::/7 and behave like private IPv4 addresses: they're for internal organization use and not intended to be routed on the public internet. A concrete example: a device might have an LLA for neighbor operations, a GUA for internet access, and a ULA for internal resources; these can coexist on the same interface. A common misconception is assuming LLAs are optional — in practice, they are foundational to local IPv6 operations. When troubleshooting, identify the prefix and then apply the correct validation steps: check RAs for GUAs, check local neighbor tables for LLAs, and treat ULAs like private addresses when diagnosing reachability beyond your administrative domain.

SLAAC lets a host create its own IPv6 address without a DHCP server. The process begins with the host generating a Link-Local Address, often using the EUI-64 method to derive a 64-bit interface identifier from the MAC address. Once the LLA exists, the host sends a Router Solicitation to discover routers on the link. A router replies with a Router Advertisement containing one or more network prefixes, for example 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64. The host then combines that advertised network prefix with its interface identifier to form a Global Unicast Address. This is stateless because routers do not keep a mapping of which host received which address; each host generates its own identifier deterministically. A common misconception is that SLAAC provides every configuration detail — it does not. SLAAC supplies the address and basic parameters, but not always DNS servers; DHCPv6 may be used in conjunction for those settings. Another frequent troubleshooting observation is a host with an LLA but no GUA; this often indicates the absence of router advertisements or misconfigured prefixes. When diagnosing SLAAC issues, confirm the presence of RAs and ensure prefix lengths like /64 are appropriate for hosts to construct valid global addresses.

EUI-64 is a deterministic method to derive a 64-bit interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC address so hosts can generate consistent IPv6 addresses. The basic steps are: split the 48-bit MAC address into two 24-bit halves, insert the fixed 16-bit sequence FFFE in the middle, and flip the seventh bit of the first byte (the Universal/Local bit). For example, given MAC 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E, you split into 001A2B and 3C4D5E, insert FFFE between them to become 001A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E, then flip the 7th bit of the first octet which changes the binary in that position to indicate local scope as needed. The result is a 64-bit interface identifier that is highly likely to be unique on the local link. One misconception is that EUI-64 always uses the MAC exactly as-is; in reality the U/L bit flip is required and insertion of FFFE is mandatory for the standard method. As a support technician, knowing EUI-64 helps you map observed interface identifiers back to device MACs when analyzing host addresses and duplicates on a link. If privacy extensions are enabled, the host may use randomized IIDs instead of EUI-64 to improve tracking resistance.

Router Advertisements are the messages routers send on a link to tell hosts about available prefixes and configuration flags. When a router advertises a prefix such as 2001:DB8:ABCD:1::/64, hosts can use SLAAC to combine that prefix with their 64-bit interface identifier — whether derived via EUI-64 or chosen by privacy extensions — to form a Global Unicast Address. The RA also includes flags that indicate whether hosts should use DHCPv6 for additional configuration or rely on SLAAC alone. A practical example: a host generates an IID and receives RA with a /64 prefix; it concatenates the prefix and IID to produce a full 128-bit address. Misunderstandings arise when the advertised prefix length is not a /64; many SLAAC implementations assume a /64 and may not form addresses if the prefix differs. As a technician, inspect RA content and prefix lengths when hosts have no GUAs or mismatched addresses. Also remember that RA-driven addresses are stateless: routers don't track who took which address. If you need centralized assignment of DNS servers or other options, DHCPv6 in stateful or stateless mode is the complement to RAs and SLAAC.

SLAAC and DHCPv6 are complementary mechanisms for IPv6 configuration. SLAAC is stateless and enables each host to construct its own address by combining an advertised prefix with an IID, while DHCPv6 provides centralized control and can operate in stateful or stateless modes. In stateful DHCPv6, the server assigns full addresses and maintains a record of leases — similar to traditional DHCP for IPv4. In stateless DHCPv6, DHCPv6 supplies auxiliary configuration like DNS servers while addresses remain SLAAC-derived. Use DHCPv6 when you require centralized assignment of DNS or strict administrative mapping of addresses. Use SLAAC when you prefer decentralized, low-overhead address configuration that scales without maintaining server-side state. A practical troubleshooting insight: if clients lack DNS information but have correct GUAs, check whether DHCPv6 is expected and whether RAs indicated that SLAAC-only should be used. Misunderstandings often arise when administrators assume SLAAC supplies DNS settings — it does not reliably do so, which is why DHCPv6 stateless mode is common for DNS provisioning. Choose the method that matches your policy and tooling, and confirm RA flags and DHCPv6 server reachability during diagnostics.

For each, omit leading zeros and compress the longest zero runs to produce an unambiguous shortened form. Task two: view IPv6 addresses on your test machine without changing configuration. On Windows run the read-only command to list interface IPv6 addresses. On Linux run the ip -6 command. The commands below are safe read-only examples you can copy into a lab terminal. When you need to practice adding or removing addresses, always do so in a virtual machine or isolated lab. The chapter supplies example commands you can use to add a test Unique Local Address for practice and then remove it. On Windows the netsh interface ipv6 add address command lets you add a ULA like FC00:DB8::10/64 to an interface named 'Ethernet' and later delete it. On Linux you can use sudo ip -6 addr add and sudo ip -6 addr del to perform the same actions against eth0. These commands change system settings, so the guidance emphasizes testing in VMs only. A typical workflow: check current addresses with the read-only command, add the temporary ULA for testing, confirm it appears, then remove it to restore the original state. A common mistake is failing to remove test addresses and leaving stale configuration on a production NIC, so always delete test addresses after verification. Use ULAs for testing to avoid accidental global routing, and record what you changed so you can revert cleanly. Practicing these steps builds confidence reading output and understanding how address lifecycles behave on real systems.

Let's recap the essential concepts you need to keep practicing. First, IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written as eight hexadecimal groups; this enormous address space removes many of the scaling problems of IPv4. Second, shortening rules let you omit leading zeros and compress one longest contiguous run of zero segments with '::' only once — misuse leads to ambiguity. Third, recognize address types by prefix: GUA (2000::/3) for global routing, LLA (FE80::/10) for link-local operations, and ULA (FC00::/7) for private internal use. Fourth, SLAAC plus EUI-64 enable stateless autoconfiguration: a host builds a link-local from its MAC, solicits routers, receives a prefix, and combines that prefix with its IID to form a global address. Finally, DHCPv6 complements SLAAC when centralized configuration or DNS assignment is needed. As you practice with the provided shortening examples and safe terminal commands, focus on identifying scope and prefix lengths — those are the fastest clues to why an IPv6 address is or isn't reachable. Keep testing in a VM and always remove test addresses after you finish.

Finish with these three compact reminders. First, always identify the prefix and scope: prefixes indicate whether the address is link-local, unique local, or globally routable, and that determination directs your troubleshooting approach. Second, apply shortening rules carefully: omit leading zeros and compress the longest zero run with a single '::'. If in doubt, expand the address to its full form to remove ambiguity. Third, know the autoconfiguration chain: a host creates a link-local address, sends a router solicitation, receives an RA with a prefix, and then forms a global address by combining the RA prefix with its IID — often derived by EUI-64. Keep using the lab exercises and read-only terminal commands to practice recognizing addresses and verifying RAs. These reminders will make it faster to spot misconfigurations and to explain IPv6 behavior clearly to users and administrators.
